claims.text: Greg LaVecchia argues that absolutism (monk mode, locking in completely) is the easier psychological route for high-achieving entrepreneurs, but it is not the route to a fulfilling and balanced life. The ease of absolutism comes from eliminating the cognitive load of moderation, but the long-run cost is estrangement from family and relationships.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
conditions: entrepreneurs who sustain extreme focus for multi-year periods (e.g. 7+ years)
claims.mechanism: Absolutism removes the daily negotiation between work and relationships, making it cognitively easier in the short run while silently accumulating relational debt that only becomes visible in retrospect.
bounded_by: Does not argue against intense focus in short sprints; argument is specific to sustained years-long extremism

claims.text: Greg LaVecchia observes that some of the best entrepreneurs he has met are a 10-out-of-10 business operator but simultaneously a poor father, son, and husband. This co-existence of professional excellence and personal failure is presented as a warning pattern, not a necessary trade-off.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
conditions: applies to founders who have adopted extreme work absolutism over long periods
bounded_by: Speaker does not claim all top entrepreneurs have this profile; he says some of the best ones do

claims.text: Greg LaVecchia applies the principle that it is easier to abstain entirely than to moderate (e.g., easier to not drink at all than to stop at two drinks) to entrepreneurship: total commitment is easier to maintain than a balanced commitment, even though balance produces better life outcomes.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
claims.mechanism: Moderation requires continuous active decisions about when to stop, while absolutism requires only one decision (always work), reducing ongoing willpower expenditure but foreclosing personal relationships.

examples.text: Greg LaVecchia reflects on his own experience of locking in for seven years straight, looking back and realizing he probably could have called his mom more often and not been so angry so much of the time. This personal retrospective is offered as evidence that sustained monk-mode absolutism extracts relational and emotional costs that are invisible in the moment but apparent in hindsight.

practices.text: Recognize that the easier psychological route (complete work absolutism) and the optimal life route are different; deliberately choose balance over ease.
